message.content:
**Logistic regression** is a statistical method used to model the relationship between one or more predictor variables and a binary (two‑class) outcome. Instead of predicting a continuous value, it predicts the probability that the outcome belongs to a particular class. ### Key features | Feature | Description | |---------|-------------| | **Outcome** | Binary (e.g., 0/1, yes/no, success/failure). | | **Model form** | Uses the logistic (sigmoid) function to map a linear combination of predictors to a probability between 0 and 1:
\(\displaystyle P(Y=1|X)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-(\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\dots+\beta_pX_p))}\) | | **Link function** | Logit link: \(\text{logit}(P)=\ln\!\big(\frac{P}{1-P}\big)=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\dots+\beta_pX_p\). | | **Estimation** | Parameters \(\beta\) are estimated by maximum likelihood (MLE). | | **Interpretation** | Coefficients represent the change in the log‑odds of the outcome per unit change in the predictor. Exponentiating gives odds ratios. | | **Assumptions** |
  • Independence of observations.
  • Linearity of the logit (predictors linearly related to log‑odds).
  • No perfect multicollinearity.
| | **Extensions** | • Multinomial logistic regression (more than two classes)
• Ordinal logistic regression (ordered categories)
• Regularized logistic regression (L1/L2 penalties) | ### Why use logistic regression? - **Interpretability**: Coefficients can be translated into odds ratios, which are intuitive for many fields (medicine, marketing, etc.). - **Probabilistic output**: Provides a probability estimate for each observation, useful for risk scoring. - **Computationally efficient**: Works well even with large datasets and high‑dimensional feature spaces. ### Example Suppose you want to predict whether a patient has a disease (1) or not (0) based on age and blood pressure: \[ \text{logit}(P)=\beta_0 + \beta_1(\text{Age}) + \beta_2(\text{BP}) \] After fitting the model, you might find: - \(\beta_1 = 0.04\) → each additional year of age increases the odds of disease by \(e^{0.04}\approx 1.04\) (4% higher). - \(\beta_2 = 0.05\) → each additional mmHg of blood pressure increases the odds by \(e^{0.05}\approx 1.05\) (5% higher). If a 60‑year‑old patient with a BP of 140 mmHg has a predicted probability of 0.30, you might classify them as “disease” if you set a threshold of 0.5, or you might use the probability directly for risk stratification. --- In short, logistic regression is a powerful, interpretable tool for binary classification that models the log‑odds of an event as a linear function of predictors.
